messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a 24-year-old urban planner who came to treatment after postponing a routine gynecologic exam for nearly a year and then leaving the clinic shaking before the physician could begin. She grew up in a home where physical abuse by her caregiver was woven into ordinary family life, often erupting in cramped domestic spaces where she was cornered, held in place, and treated less like a child than like something to be managed. She remembers hands directing her body, the humiliation of being watched for signs of defiance, and the sick, rolling nausea that would come before she was grabbed. What remains most vivid is not a clear sequence but the bodily certainty of exposure and helplessness. Even as a girl she learned that the safest way through these moments was to stay agreeable, move carefully, and give the adult what was wanted before the adult’s mood shifted.

In the years since leaving home, Linh has had difficulty calling up the abuse deliberately. When she tries to remember in a linear way, her mind seems to go blank around the worst parts. Yet the emotional force is immediate. A medical examination table, the sound of gloves snapping on, or simply feeling nauseous can bring a surge of the same dread without a full picture attached; at other times, if she is caught off guard by being looked at too closely, she is hit by intense anger that feels out of proportion to the present moment until she recognizes that it belongs to something older. These moments do not arrive as coherent memories so much as a flood of feeling, and that very fragmentariness has hardened her sense that what happened was deeply unfair and never answered for. When the feelings come without images, she is left with the conviction that she had been reduced to an object in someone else’s control, and with a familiar, shaming conclusion that a stronger person would somehow not still react this way.

That belief has shaped how narrowly she now organizes her life. Linh says she only really feels safe in her apartment and in one corner workstation at the planning office, where she can see who is approaching. Sudden movements by coworkers—a hand reaching across her desk, a chair pushed back quickly in a meeting—make her body tense before she can think. On those days she finds it hard to concentrate on zoning maps and public comments, scanning the room instead of tracking details. Living so much on guard has made ordinary exposures feel increasingly loaded: being seen while presenting at work, sitting in a waiting room knowing she may be examined, even noticing a wave of nausea on the subway can register as signs that something is about to happen. At that pitch of alertness, the range of things that can function as warnings widens quickly; a coworker leaning over her shoulder, the rustle of a paper gown from an exam room down the hall, even the churn in her own stomach are taken up by her body as reminders before she has time to think about them. Feeling this endangered so often has also become, in her mind, its own kind of proof: if she still has to move through the world this braced and vigilant, she takes it as evidence that she really is weak, easily overpowered, and permanently changed by what was done to her. When she is keyed up like this, the old abuse is much harder to hold at a distance; the sense that danger is close seems to pull up the same bodily memory with it, so that a tense commute or crowded meeting can suddenly fill with the helplessness and exposure of those earlier moments. The more vigilant she becomes, the smaller her safe world gets, and the more quickly she reads movement, scrutiny, and bodily discomfort as danger.

In those moments Linh falls back on strategies that once protected her. If a supervisor asks for a last-minute change, she agrees immediately even when it creates extra work, because going along feels safer than risking disapproval. Because she so rarely stays in these situations long enough to discover that nothing worse is about to happen, the danger never has a chance to recede for her; the very strategies that help her get through the moment keep her body convinced the threat is current and real. Over time these habits have made reminders more pervasive rather than less; the clinic she keeps canceling, the site visits she turns down, and even the careful way she positions herself at her workstation have each become small daily markers of what must be avoided. Each time she gets through the day by appeasing, canceling, or disappearing, it leaves behind the same conclusion: that she must not be capable of coping directly, or she would not need so many maneuvers just to feel minimally safe. At medical appointments she becomes compliant to the point of disappearance, then cancels follow-ups rather than face another reminder. When friends ask about her childhood, she changes the subject or stops returning messages for a while. Triggers pull her toward these habits: being examined, feeling watched, or getting nauseous makes her want to placate, avoid, and mentally drift into thoughts about how different her life might have been if she had grown up in a home where she was protected. Those counterfactual loops briefly take her out of the room, but they also keep the abuse emotionally active. Afterward she is more likely to be ambushed by the same free-floating intensity or by flashes of rage, and more likely to come away believing again that she is weak for still arranging her life around something she can barely describe.

Her beliefs and coping now feed each other in ways she can feel but has never put into words. Because she has come to see herself as someone who is fundamentally weak and easily overpowered, she people-pleases preemptively and avoids reminders before they can expose that weakness. Each retreat leaves her more confined and watchful, which makes concentration harder and keeps her alert to sudden movements and scrutiny. The more she lives this way, the more often nausea, examinations, and being seen set off the old emotional storm. Then the memory returns in its familiar fractured form—feeling without picture, rage without a full scene—and again confirms for her that she was dehumanized and that no one ever made it right.

What finally brought Linh in was a convergence of work and health. She had started declining site visits because crowded public meetings and unpredictable jostling left her too keyed up to focus, and her manager had noticed. At the same time, another missed medical appointment left her frightened by how completely she had shut down in the clinic. She is seeking help now because she is tired of living inside such a small radius of safety. What frightens her most is the possibility that this is simply who she is—weak, easily controlled, never fully a person in her own mind. What she hopes, cautiously, is that she might learn to be in her body, at work, and in a doctor’s office without feeling she has already lost herself.
